title: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
description: Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to
body: Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court.The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars."Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said."Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added. The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer. Farah Naz, the aunt of Zara Aleena who was sexually assaulted and murdered as she was walking home in Ilford, east London, in June 2022, said her niece's murderer refusing to come to court for sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".She said Zara's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer Jordan McSweeney, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused". McSweeney was jailed for at least 38 years."Taking away these privileges... would rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim," Naz said.Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing. For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions. But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves". The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws. All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings. Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice". She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

schema.headline: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits

title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
description: After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackda
body: After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding housed in the National Wealth Fund.A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go? It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time."The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said."If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth. The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's. "Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era. The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories. Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund. Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic. It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future. While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that. Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

schema.headline: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built

title: Dame Judi Dench: I can't do a play, do a film, or read any more
description: Dame Judi also discussed meeting US actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.She was appea
body: Dame Judi also discussed meeting US actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door.She said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling."Asked what she had said to him, Dame Judi replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall."The conversation then turned to her love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine."He walked on and he said, 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'Oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?"She also admitted to being "besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them.""It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added. "It's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."

schema.headline: Dame Judi Dench: I can't do a play, do a film, or read any more

title: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study
description: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.It will
body: A clinical trial has been launched in the UK which scientists hope could cut years from the search for new treatments for Alzheimer's disease.It will test multiple drugs simultaneously, starting with two repurposed medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).The study will examine whether the drugs can lessen symptoms such as memory and thinking problems, and help people maintain their quality of life.Angela Bucksey, 67, from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in January and is the first person to begin treatment on the trial, called AD-SMART."We have Alzheimer's in the family," she told the BBC."My mother had it and my aunts, so it was a disappointment rather than a shock when I was diagnosed because I knew it would restrict my life."But I was determined that it wasn't going to define me."Angela said she felt empowered joining the trial because "at least you are doing something"."Instead of just sitting there, you're standing up and saying, I will fight back."Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father died from Alzheimer's last month, said he knew how it felt to lose a loved one to dementia, and had seen first-hand the devastating impact of the disease on families."That's why I'm proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible," he said.The AD-SMART study is what's known as a multi-arm, multi-stage platform trial where several treatments are tested simultaneously, with the results compared with one group of participants taking a placebo or dummy.This means those involved have a higher likelihood of getting an active treatment than in a traditional trial.If any drug isn't showing benefit it can be dropped quickly and a new treatment added in its place - the approach has been used successfully in cancer and motor neurone disease.The two initial drugs being tested are metformin, used to treat type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, for ADHD, which were selected by an international panel of experts.Both drugs may help reduce brain inflammation, which is a driver of neurodegeneration, said chief investigator Prof Paresh Malhotra, group leader at the UK Dementia Research Institute Centre for Care Research & Technology at Imperial College London."For too long, Alzheimer's research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer - sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we've found something that works," he told the BBC."We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer's disease."For the drugs to be successful, the study has to show that they have beneficial effects on thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities."That's what patients and their carers care about," said Prof Malhotra.Some 1,200 participants with mild to moderate Alzheimer's will be recruited at more than 30 sites across the UK. Sites in Cambridgeshire, Surrey, London, Southampton and Edinburgh are already open.Scientists expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030 and, in that time, additional treatments are likely to be added.All the participants will have regular health checks including cognitive tests, which will help researchers assess how effective the treatments are.Angela Bucksey's husband Steve, who is her study partner, told the BBC: "Joining the trial has brought us back from the despair of a diagnosis which everybody recognises is non-recoverable."People who know we are on a drug trial understand that we're doing something about it and, rather than be sorry for us, they can be encouraging."Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer's Research UK said "time is precious" for people living with Alzheimer's disease and more treatment options are urgently needed.People with a confirmed Alzheimer's diagnosis who would like to take part can register their interest on the AD-SMART website, external.The trial is being led by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer's Research UK.Partners include the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Medical Research Council and Health Data Research UK, with funding by UK government.

schema.headline: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

title: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 2 hours agoFor more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 2 hours agoFor more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".What is the flaw?Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.What websites have been affected?The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.  That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.Image source, EPAImage caption, Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on WednesdayA number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.What happened after the flaws were exposed?Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database."These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X. "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.How is AI finding weak spots?The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said. "The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure."Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.What can people do to safeguard themselves?Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said.The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors."Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

schema.headline: PHP: What is it and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

title: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029
description: The four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations
body: The four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations to be the next UK City of CultureBySteven McIntosh and Ian YoungsBlackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029. The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.The shortlisted cities are:Image source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."Milton KeynesImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."SheffieldImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London.What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans".Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are."WrexhamImage source, Getty ImagesWhat is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place."Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous."Get in touchDo you live in one of the shortlisted cities? What do you love about your city?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: UK City of Culture: Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham shortlisted for 2029

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
description: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East corre
body: Image caption, Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's electionByYolande KnellMiddle East correspondentReporting fromNazarethAt rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties."I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."Image caption, All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab partiesMost opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.Image caption, Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity.  Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.Image caption, Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab partiesAt Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party. I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties."In a word its racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings. These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.Image caption, United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc. For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government."We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me. "That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Joint List talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace Netanyahu's governmentMeanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition. It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime. In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for. Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.Image caption, Arab Israelis accuse the government of inaction on the issue of gang crimeIn Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November. No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction."It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness.""As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."Image source, Ziad SamouniImage caption, Ziad Samouni's son Hussein (2nd L) was shot dead last November but no arrests have been made This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

schema.headline: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election

title: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad
description: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth
body: The grads ditching the UK for a fresh start abroadImage caption, Charlie West, left, Rachel James and Owein Iveson have all moved overseasByElizabeth AndersonBusiness reporterLast year Rachel James quit her corporate job in London, packed a suitcase and booked a one-way ticket to Sydney, without a job lined up or a plan in place."I went for a fresh start," says the 26-year-old from Surrey. "To take a risk and try something completely different. With the worst case being there will always be a flight home if all fails."More than one in 10 UK university students are now planning to move abroad for better opportunities after they have graduated, up from 7.8% two years ago, according to a survey, external of 15,000 final year university students.Meanwhile, a study by the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) says that competition for graduate jobs in the UK was at a three-decade high. UK employers now receive 140 applications per graduate vacancy on average, an increase of 14% from 2025, and up from just 30 applications per vacancy 20 years ago, according to the ISE's report, external.For young British adults going abroad, where are they heading?Australia: 'The weather's beautiful, even in the winter'While there is no age-specific data for which countries people go to, Australia remains by far the most popular nation for British adults overall who move abroad, official figures show., externalIn addition to Australia's weather and use of the English language, another reason is its visa-friendly policy. Under its Working Holiday Maker programme,, external British passport holders between the ages of 18 and 35 can live in Australia for up to three years.Image source, Rachel JamesImage caption, Rachel James says that Sydney is a nicer place to live and work than LondonRachel, who graduated from Loughborough University in 2022 with a degree in English, had been working for accountancy giant PricewaterhouseCoopers in the UK. She now has a job in marketing in Sydney for gym chain Fitness First.She says her annual salary has gone down from £42,000 to £37,000, while she now pays $AUS 2,000 (£1,000) a month to rent a two-bedroom apartment with a friend, similar to what she was paying in London.Despite having less disposable income, she has no regrets. "The weather's beautiful, even in the winter, and the walks on my doorstep are unmatched."People want to leave work at 5pm so they can go and do their hobbies - whether it's surfing, running, enjoying the sunset, a picnic or sunset yoga. I didn't come with career progression as a focus - it's more about the different way of life."The US: 'I'm paid a lot more here'Around two-thirds of British nationals who emigrate are aged between 16 and 34, according to the most recent figures, external from the UK's Office for National Statistics.It said that 75,000 more people in that age bracket left the UK in 2025 than arrived.After Australia the next most popular destination for British adults is the US.Image source, Charlie WestImage caption, Charlie West says that working in the US has given him better pay and more opportunitiesCharlie West, 25, from Cheshire, moved to the States in 2024 for better pay and opportunities in academia after he completed a masters in medieval studies at Oxford University.West is now two years in to a six-year funded PhD course at Yale's Department of Italian Studies, which includes him teaching."I really wanted to do a PhD but it's difficult to get funding in the UK, particularly in the humanities, and funded stipends are about £21,000. I'd have had to work [outside academia] at the same time to afford to live."In the US I'm paid $51,000 a year (£37,770), about to rise to $52,000, and it comes with a lot more opportunities to teach and travel to conferences."Europe: 'If you can work across the EU there are more opportunities'The European Union also remains popular with young Britons looking to move abroad, although the visa requirements since Brexit have made it more difficult.One way to get into the European jobs market is to have studied in the EU. International graduates can apply for a permanent residence permit after their degree ends.Image source, Owein IvesonImage caption, Owein Iveson has no plans to return to the UK from FinlandThis is what Owein Iveson, 24, from Sunderland, is doing as he is about to graduate from Finland's Aalto University with a masters in design.Owein says he "fell in love with the country" after visiting for the first time in 2020."Finland's a beautiful country," he says. "The streets are very clean. It's a very quiet lifestyle. The nature is fantastic and the public transport works really efficiently."Owein lives in Espoo, a city about 15 minutes on the metro from Helsinki, and doesn't expect to return to the UK anytime soon."To be honest the jobs market is not great in Finland, but there is high demand for IT workers, and if you can work across the EU there are many more opportunities."Immigration lawyer John Kiely, a London-based partner at international law firm Howard Kennedy, says it is easy to see why more UK graduates are looking overseas. "When you combine student debt, high housing costs, relatively weak wage growth and uncertainty about future employment, the willingness to roll the dice somewhere else becomes quite rational."Back in Sydney, Rachel says the city simply offers a better quality of life than London. "I don't see life in Sydney as any more expensive than if I was in London, but personally I have found the perks in Sydney better."

schema.headline: The graduates ditching the UK to work abroad

title: Bayern Munich: 'Ridiculous' Harry Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
description: Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive.There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling
body: Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive.There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League when the forward took matters into his own hands in a bid to break the deadlock.As the Premier League champions prepared to defend a Bayern goal-kick, Kane seized the initiative by launching his side up the pitch with a raking 80-yard pass.It was a moment of remarkable ingenuity from the England international, one that almost ended with Bayern taking the lead."Under Vincent Kompany, he has been given a level of trust that he has probably never had before under any other manager," former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport."For all the things we've seen him do and the positions we've seen him roam into, nobody has seen him take a goal-kick before."But even someone like Manuel Neuer, who is his senior and has been at Bayern for a large part of his career, sees Harry Kane put the ball down and thinks, 'OK, sure'. He lets Harry go for it because he thinks whatever he sees is going to be correct."At the same time, there were Bayern players running forward because they knew that the ball could come."For him to be taking a goal-kick is not something you may want to see very often. You don't necessarily want your number nine to be THAT deep, but the nature of his game when he is playing for Bayern is to roam, and today it was a huge benefit to the team."Although Kane was denied the opportunity to add another outstanding assist to his already impressive catalogue, he did not have to wait long to make another decisive contribution.After Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead, Kane helped Bayern restore parity, bending a sumptuous pass around Jurrien Timber for Alphonso Davies to finish.The England captain then fired the hosts in front from the penalty spot midway through the second half, taking his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.But Declan Rice struck late on to earn Arsenal a share of the spoils.For Kane, it was another mesmerising performance that underlined his credentials as the frontrunner for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.The former Tottenham Hotspur captain, 33, could become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the prestigious individual award, with Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Paris St-Germain forward and current holder Ousmane Dembele among the favourites.Kane was named on the 30-man shortlist in September, with the winner due to be announced on Monday following a vote by an international jury of 100 journalists."He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he has had has been remarkable," Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice told TNT Sports."When you play with him, you realise how good he is, and when you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is."He is ridiculous, such a good player, and I am lucky I can play with him, not so lucky I have to play against him."By scoring against Arsenal on Wednesday night, Kane became only the second player in Champions League history to find the net in 10 consecutive matches.The only other player to achieve the feat was five-time Ballon d'Or winner Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 successive matches for Real Madrid between June 2017 and April 2018."Kane certainly looks at home at Bayern. He understands the team and its system, and they all understand him. They know that when he gets the ball at his feet, wherever that may be, something good can happen," Onuoha added."I think all the Bayern players are really playing into that, but then Harry steps up and scores a penalty as well."Having freedom is probably the best way to describe what he has got playing for Bayern, because he will work hard defensively, which allows him the freedom to be creative when he is in attack. For now, he certainly is thriving."Kane's goal against Arsenal took his tally to 156 in 158 appearances since joining Bayern Munich from Tottenham in 2023.It was another night to remember for the England captain, but the best could yet be to come, with the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London looming."It would be amazing to win," said Kane afterwards. "The voting closed a long time ago so there's nothing I can do, just wait and see what happens."

schema.headline: Bayern Munich: 'Ridiculous' Harry Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials

title: Devon and Cornwall battens down the hatches before Storm Austen
description: Extra safety measures have been set up by people and businesses as they prepare for the UK's first named storm of the season.Storm Austen is forecast
body: Extra safety measures have been set up by people and businesses as they prepare for the UK's first named storm of the season.Storm Austen is forecast to bring gusts of up to 80mph (130km/h) and heavy rain across parts of Cornwall and Devon from Thursday night, according to the Met Office.The conditions, which are also set to affect parts of Wales, England's south coast, Wiltshire and Somerset, have led to two weather warnings being issued, external for Friday.Bosses at The Watering Hole bar on Perranporth Beach in Cornwall said they were taking extra precautions after the venue suffered damage during Storm Goretti in January.Jamie-Lee Job said the bar lost several glass panels during that storm as the wind physically lifted them up and sent them crashing through a roof canopy.Ahead of Storm Austen, staff at the bar have been fixing parts of the building down to make them more secure."It was quite scary, we've survived a lot of storms but that particular storm we underestimated how bad it was going to be," Job said."It is a reminder to us all to best err on the side of caution."So for this one we are doing everything we can do to make sure everything is secure and hopefully the roof stays on for this one."Other people in Perranporth said they had stocked up on supplies in case they lost power during Storm Austen.Chris Eves said: "We've got loads of torches and candles and lots of flasks so we should be OK."Another woman who was walking along the town's beach said she was preparing to "hunker down".She added: "I've got lots of candles, we've got a rechargeable radio, rechargeable lights, a gas-fired pizza oven and I am thinking about buying a primus stove as well."I am also thinking I won't have anything expensive in my freezer, so if there's a power cut I won't lose too much."Cornwall Council has issued a warning urging people to prepare before the storm hits and to avoid exposed coastal areas on Thursday evening and Friday."Strong winds and large waves could make conditions extremely dangerous," the council said.Camborne Rugby Club said it would be closing its club grounds for at least 24 hours from 15:00 on Thursday, while its clubhouse would be shut from about 22:00.Meanwhile, Newquay Business Improvement District said it had cancelled Saturday's Zombie Crawl parade due to the weather forecast.The RNLI has reminded those along the coast to exercise "extreme caution if visiting the shoreline, especially along exposed cliffs and seafronts".Appledore RNLI Coxswain Simon McCarthy said his crew was ready to go out "at any time" and was securing its boats with extra lashings while monitoring the storm.  "With the amber warning, it means the all-weather lifeboats are more called upon," McCarthy explained.  "The inshore boats have got their limitations, so we have to make sure we have crew available."He added: "We really do want people to be sensible. The sea will always win."Devon County Council said it would have extra staff on hand in its Network Operations Control Centre to monitor conditions and co-ordinate responses to any weather-related incidents.Councillor Dan Thomas, cabinet member for highways, said: "We're preparing for a spell of unsettled weather and would encourage everyone travelling around Devon to keep an eye on the forecast and plan ahead."With many trees still in leaf following the dry weather, there is a risk of fallen trees and branches on our roads."Dartmouth Food Festival has also been impacted by the storm with organisers pushing some events planned for Friday back to Saturday morning.Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

title: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds
description: Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.A Cambrid
body: Rosalind Franklin is the only female scientist named in GCSE and National 5 science exam specifications in the UK, according to new research.A Cambridge study found that of the 86 scientists named by UK exam boards, the English chemist, whose work in the 1950s helped reveal the structure of DNA, was the only woman.Exam specifications set out the skills and knowledge students are expected to have gained by the end of their course and how they will be assessed.Exam boards said there was "a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications".Academics from the University of Cambridge, along with institutions in the US and Australia, examined how many women were mentioned in specifications for biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, geology and astronomy.Their work, published in the British Educational Research Journal, looked at six exam boards in the UK:AQACambridge OCRPearson EdexcelWJECCCEAQualifications ScotlandAt Key Stage 4 and equivalent, including GCSEs and National 5s in Scotland, Franklin was the only woman among the 86 scientists mentioned.She was also one of three women mentioned at Key Stage 5 and equivalent - including A-levels, AS-levels, National Highers and National Advanced Highers - out of a total of 181 scientists.Marie Tharp, an American cartographer who created the first map of the floor of the Atlantic ocean in the 1950s, and Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist who discovered the existence of the Earth's inner core in the 1930s, both feature in the Cambridge OCR's A-­level Geology.Franklin, who was named in Cambridge OCR's GCSE Biology and Scottish Highers Biology, produced a famous DNA image known as Photograph 51.Cambridge scientists Francis Crick and James Watson used the image to work out the following year that DNA has a double-helix structure.Watson, Crick and Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery. Franklin had died four years earlier.Academics who wrote the paper found that "several major scientific breakthroughs" in specifications were made by women, but they were not explicitly mentioned.The paper said: "Many of the scientific discoveries and explanations were developed in the 1800s and early 1900s, a period when scientific and mathematical practice was largely, but not solely, dominated by men. "Our findings confirm that the UK science specifications reflect this historical imbalance: although women made significant contributions to major scientific breakthroughs, this fact is rarely acknowledged."The academics recommended that Franklin should be included "in all specifications when teaching DNA structure".They also said specifications should refer to Marie Curie, who discovered radium and polonium and coined the term radioactivity, and nuclear physicist Lise Meitner, who discovered nuclear fission, among others.Stephanie Buttigieg, one of the authors, said: "Relatable role models can help keep more girls in STEM by strengthening their sense of belonging in science and fostering positive attitudes towards scientific careers."A spokeswoman for the Joint Council for Qualifications, which represents AQA, Cambridge OCR, CCEA, WJEC and Pearson, said: "Exam boards recognise that there is a clear need for greater representation in science qualifications, and this is an area they will be focusing on as these qualifications are reformed."Qualifications Scotland said the Curriculum Improvement Cycle offered "an opportunity to consider gender representation within our future qualifications and assessments". The Department for Education in England said "girls should see the contribution women have made in STEM", adding it was "committed to improving the school curriculum over the coming years, and as part of that will make sure every girl can see where their learning can take them".The Scottish Government said it was "committed to closing the gender gap in STEM and will carefully consider the findings of this research".Additional reporting by Marthe de Ferrer and Rahib Khan

schema.headline: Only one female scientist named in GCSEs, research finds

title: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)BySteve RosenbergRussia EditorReporting fromMoscowAfter two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard."In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace."I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said,  "but things are moving in that direction."All rather vague.It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken holdIn recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader."Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says."Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?""Of course!"A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe."Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push

title: Bruno Fernandes rounds on Michael Carrick after Man Utd lose to Como in Champions League
description: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Ferna
body: Figure caption, Man Utd humbled by four-goal Como to pile pressure on CarrickByManchester United reporter in ComoManchester United captain Bruno Fernandes turned on head coach Michael Carrick following one of the most humiliating nights in the club's European history.A 4-1 Champions League hammering at Como led to Carrick fielding questions about his future.He apologised to the 700 travelling fans, having ignored his beaten players after the final whistle to march across the pitch and repeatedly hold his hands up - in a manner similar to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer following a 4-1 defeat at Watford in November 2021 which led to his dismissal as United boss 24 hours later.However, Fernandes - widely accepted as a football obsessive who watches games regularly and understands the tactical side as well as any player in the United squad - inflicted more damage when he spoke to TNT Sports afterwards."It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confidence," he said.Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: "That's on the manager and staff to see it, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."Figure caption, 'That is on the manager' - Fernandes on Man Utd tacticsCarrick avoids questions on future, apologises to fans for unacceptable displayCarrick also refused to answer questions about his own future.Instead, he described his own feelings about United's performance and focused on taking responsibility."I have to apologise to the supporters," said the former player. "I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more, with the position that I'm in and what I value this football club. For us to play in that way is not acceptable."I always go over to the fans anyway, regardless, so it wasn't a particularly different kind of reason why I went over."It's the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they've gone through and have done over a period of a few weeks now. As I said, I was one of them."I'm feeling the same as them. We've got a lot of values in this football club; what we represent and how we want to go about it. We might win, we might lose, but the way we went about it tonight wasn't acceptable. I just wanted to let the fans know that I feel for them."Listen. I've not given my own position any thought - this is for the supporters - I was one of them watching that and I wasn't happy all."Figure caption, Carrick responds to Fernandes criticism on tacticsSeven without a win - Man Utd's bleak pictureAfter winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season to guide United back into the Champions League after a two-year absence, Carrick was given a two-year contract.However, as happened with Solskjaer five years ago, the new campaign has unravelled spectacularly and they are 13th in the Premier League, three points clear of bottom club Sunderland.Although they recovered from their shock opening-day defeat to newly promoted Hull by coming from behind to beat Ipswich the following week, United have not won in the Premier League since. Their only other success in 11 games in all competitions came against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.Their latest loss meant they have now gone seven games without a win, their worst run since they went eight without a victory under Louis van Gaal between 25 November and 28 December 2015.Only Joshua Zirkzee's injury-time consolation prevented United suffering their joint second-worst European defeat of all time.The embarrassment was heightened by the knowledge that when they were last crowned European champions in 2008, Como were playing semi-professional football in front of a couple of hundred spectators in Serie D.It is a basic reality that if Como's star man Nico Paz, who opened the scoring after 118 seconds, created the second and added a third goal, said he wanted to leave Como, virtually every big club in Europe would want to sign him and United's chances would be virtually non-existent.They entertain 15th-placed Bournemouth in the Premier League on Sunday knowing that prior to last season's amazing 4-4 draw, the Cherries recorded 3-0 wins on their previous two visits to Old Trafford.Figure caption, Carrick 'bitterly disappointed' by Man Utd peformanceWhat happens now?United flew straight back to Manchester after the game.It remains to be seen whether the position around Carrick changes before the Bournemouth game. However, United supporters sang against the Glazer family and Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the shambolic evening unravelled. Both Carrick and sporting director Jason Wilcox have been absolved of partial blame for the club's plight by some; Carrick because he was let down badly in the summer transfer window, when the club signed three midfielders, but failed to bring in competition for Luke Shaw at left-back and Benjamin Sesko in attack. Wilcox too, because he had to work to a budget set by those above him, including chief executive Omar Berrada."There was a lot going through my mind watching that," admitted Carrick, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League during his United playing career. "It was tough to watch."It wasn't just the goals, if I'm totally honest. It was was the manner and way we played at times."I'm giving my absolute best all the time, I care about it. My whole life is wrapped around it. It might go well, it might not go so well, but I I genuinely give everything that I possibly can."Figure caption, Man Utd fans on if Carrick should stayFollow Manchester United on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical United contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about the Red Devils

title: Women take to social media to break the taboo of UTIs
description: "The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells
body: "The impact goes far beyond what people understand - we're talking about pain, urgency, sleepless nights and missing out on your life," Adrianne tells her roughly 8,000 followers in a video on TikTok.For nearly five years, Adrianne has lived with a chronic urinary tract infection (UTI) - a condition it took her two years to get a diagnosis for.In that time she was wrongly told it was colon cancer, Crohn's disease or even that her partner must have been cheating and had given her a sexually transmitted infection.What started as one UTI in 2022 became a debilitating cycle."It has completely stripped me of everything: being able to work properly, my relationships, my friendships, going out, being able to have a normal social life," says Adrianne, who works in digital marketing in London.The 29-year-old was eventually diagnosed privately with a chronic UTI - something experts estimate could affect up to 1.7 million women in the UK, external. Men and children are also affected.Adrianne is not alone in sharing her story and coping mechanisms on social media to fight the stigma surrounding UTIs.A quick search on Tiktok or Instagram shows hundreds of posts of women of all ages talking about the reality of living with recurrent and chronic UTIs."I felt incredibly nervous to put myself out there, but there's now this community of people who can share tips with each other, and understand each other," said Adrianne, saying her posts have had a "really positive response"."It's very validating."While sending a urine sample to the lab remains the gold standard to diagnose a UTI, "false negatives" can often occur, says Professor Chris Harding, a consultant urologist at Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.Another hurdle is the significant crossover between chronic UTIs and other conditions such as painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic pain and endometriosis, says Magda Kujawa, a consultant urologist at Stockport NHS Foundation Trust.Adrianne says she felt "dismissed" by doctors while trying to get a diagnosis, and frustrated at repeatedly being given advice around hygiene and hydration, while her symptoms persisted.Both experts say health professionals should listen to the patient's story to understand whether symptoms amount to a recurrent or chronic condition or something else entirely.Since she started posting online, Adrianne has received messages from other young women who worry they are "dirty" and "not taking care of themselves" or that there is "something wrong with them". "There's definitely still a lot of stigma around why people get them (UTIs), and it all just comes back to education. We're not taught about them at school," she adds.Laura Von Müllen, 26, has also been diagnosed with a chronic UTI and documents her experience on TikTok.She says her symptoms "really badly" impacted university, and became particularly difficult to manage when she started working. She now works remotely from Kent doing social media management.As well as urinary symptoms, Laura says she also experiences heart palpitations and panic attacks."People don't understand, they think it's just a UTI and that it'll clear within three days, but I've still got mine two years later," she says.Laura also feels there is still a lot of misconception around UTIs. "People have said to me: who have you been sleeping with then? When that's not the case."Adrianne and Laura hope more women sharing their experience will help demystify the condition.Harding agrees. adding that "the more we can talk about these conditions, the more people will present to appropriate specialists and get the right treatment."But both Harding and Kujawa warn that while social media can be a useful resource, there is the risk of coming across misinformation and harmful advice, including "hacks" that could cause more harm. "I've seen women on social media sitting in baths of disinfectant, all because they were convinced that that they were dirty, and that's why they were getting infections. And actually, that just made things ten times worse," Kujawa says.While Adrianne and Laura's symptoms are showing improvements, they say it's a "long road to recovery".

schema.headline: Women take to social media to break the taboo of UTIs
